title: Cross the Shibuya scramble at rush hour
description: Up to three thousand people cross at once when the lights change. The Starbucks window above it is the free viewing gallery.

title: Get to Senso-ji before the shutters go up
description: Tokyo's oldest temple, founded in 628. At six in the morning the approach is empty and the smoke from the incense cauldron is yours alone.

title: Eat sushi for breakfast at Toyosu
description: The tuna auction moved here from Tsukiji in 2018. Viewing from the deck is free; the sushi counters upstairs open at five.

title: Walk the Meiji Jingu forest in the middle of the city
description: A hundred thousand trees donated from across Japan in 1920 and planted to become a forest. It worked.

title: Drink in a Golden Gai bar the size of a cupboard
description: Two hundred bars in six alleys, most seating five or six people. Many charge a cover; the ones that welcome visitors say so on the door.

title: Look down on Tokyo for free from the Metropolitan Building
description: Two hundred and two metres up, no charge, and on a clear winter morning Mount Fuji is visible from the north tower.

title: See the Ghibli Museum in Mitaka
description: Tickets go on sale on the tenth of the month before and sell out the same day. No photography inside, deliberately.

title: Watch a sumo morning practice
description: Stables allow a small number of visitors to sit silently at the edge of morning training. Tournaments are only six times a year; this is not.

title: Walk from Yanaka cemetery through old Shitamachi
description: One of the few districts to survive both the 1923 earthquake and the firebombing, so the wooden houses and shopping street are original.

title: Walk up through the Fushimi Inari gates at dawn
description: Ten thousand vermilion torii up a mountain, each donated by a business. Open all night; go at five and you will meet almost no one.

title: Stand under the Arashiyama bamboo before seven
description: The sound of the stalks knocking together is on Japan's official list of soundscapes to preserve, and you can only hear it early.

title: See Kinkaku-ji reflected in its pond
description: Two floors covered in gold leaf, burned down by a monk in 1950 and rebuilt. Best after snow, which Kyoto gets a few days a year.

title: Sit in front of the rock garden at Ryoan-ji
description: Fifteen stones in raked gravel, arranged so you can never see all fifteen at once from the veranda. Nobody agrees what it means.

title: Walk the Philosopher's Path in cherry blossom
description: Two kilometres of canal lined with cherry trees, named for a philosopher who walked it daily to Kyoto University.

title: Eat kaiseki in a Kyoto machiya
description: A multi-course seasonal meal that is the formal end of Japanese cooking. Book weeks ahead; many places take no walk-ins.

title: Take part in a tea ceremony properly
description: Uji has grown the country's best matcha since the twelfth century. A full ceremony runs to a script and takes real time.

title: Bow to the deer at Nara Park
description: Twelve hundred wild sika deer that will bow back if you bow first. They are wild animals and will also take your map.

title: Stand under the Great Buddha at Todai-ji
description: Fifteen metres of bronze in what was the largest wooden building in the world until 1998, and is still enormous.

title: Eat takoyaki and kushikatsu in Dotonbori
description: Osaka's word for eating yourself broke is kuidaore, and this is where it happens. Never double-dip the kushikatsu sauce.

title: Cross the floating garden at Umeda Sky Building
description: Two towers joined by a doughnut-shaped roof deck 170 metres up, reached by an escalator through open air.

title: Climb the keep at Himeji Castle
description: The finest surviving Japanese castle, never burned or bombed, with six storeys of steep wooden stairs to the top.

title: Walk the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route
description: A thousand-year-old pilgrimage through cedar forest, and one of only two pilgrim routes in the world with world heritage status.

title: Stay overnight in a temple on Koyasan
description: Sleep in a working monastery, eat shojin ryori and attend the dawn service. Okunoin cemetery at night is the reason to stay.

title: Climb Mount Fuji overnight for the sunrise
description: The official season is barely two months. Huts must be booked, and altitude catches out people who treated it as a walk.

title: See Fuji from Lake Kawaguchi in the morning
description: The mountain hides behind cloud most summer days. Winter mornings are clear, and the reflection in the lake is why people come.

title: Watch the snow monkeys bathe at Jigokudani
description: Japanese macaques that learned to sit in a hot spring. A 1.6-kilometre walk in through snow, and the monkeys ignore you entirely.

title: Walk the Azusa river at Kamikochi
description: A closed valley in the Northern Alps with no private cars, clear water and the Hotaka range standing over it.

title: See the thatched gassho houses at Shirakawa-go
description: Steep-roofed farmhouses built to shed four metres of snow, some three hundred years old and still lived in.

title: Walk the old merchant streets of Takayama
description: Dark timber sake breweries and morning markets in a mountain town that the modern railway reached late and lightly.

title: See Kenroku-en in every season
description: One of Japan's three great gardens. In winter the pines are hung with rope cones to stop the snow breaking them.

title: Walk the snow corridor on the Alpine Route
description: Snow walls up to twenty metres high, cut through each spring by ploughs, on a route crossed by cable car, bus and trolley.

title: See the lavender fields of Furano
description: Hokkaido's brief summer turns these hills purple for about four weeks. The Farm Tomita fields are the ones in the photographs.

title: Ski the powder at Niseko
description: Siberian air crossing the Sea of Japan dumps fifteen metres of dry snow a season here. It is why Australians learned to ski in Japan.

title: Look for brown bears in Shiretoko
description: A peninsula at the far north-east with one of the densest brown bear populations on earth, reached mostly by boat.

title: Walk the Sapporo Snow Festival sculptures
description: Two hundred snow and ice sculptures along Odori Park each February, some of them the size of buildings.

title: Walk the beech forest of Shirakami-Sanchi
description: The last large virgin beech forest in East Asia, world heritage listed, with almost no trails through the core.

title: See the gold hall at Chuson-ji
description: A twelfth-century hall covered inside and out in gold leaf, protected within a concrete shell, in the far north.

title: Take the boat through the pines of Matsushima bay
description: Two hundred and sixty pine-covered islets, ranked one of Japan's three great views since the seventeenth century.

title: Climb the thousand steps at Yamadera
description: A temple complex up a cliff, reached by 1,015 stone steps through cedar. Basho wrote a famous haiku here about the silence.

title: Stand in the Peace Memorial Park
description: The dome was left standing as it was on 6 August 1945. The museum next to it is unsparing and should be done slowly.

title: See the Itsukushima torii at high tide
description: The gate appears to float when the tide is in and you can walk out to it when it is out. Check the tide table before the ferry.

title: Cycle the art islands of Naoshima
description: A former industrial island turned over to Tadao Ando museums and a Yayoi Kusama pumpkin on the jetty.

title: Walk the Tottori sand dunes
description: Sixteen kilometres of coastal dunes up to fifty metres high, the largest in Japan, with camels for hire at the edge.

title: Visit Izumo Taisha, where the gods gather
description: The oldest shrine in Japan, where all eight million gods are said to meet each October. You clap four times here, not two.

title: Walk part of the 88-temple Shikoku pilgrimage
description: Twelve hundred kilometres around an island, walked in white with a staff. Most people do it in sections over years.

title: Eat tonkotsu ramen at a Fukuoka yatai
description: Open-air food stalls that set up on the riverbank each evening. Fukuoka is where the pork bone broth comes from.

title: Bathe in a Beppu onsen
description: More hot spring water comes out of the ground here than anywhere on earth except Yellowstone. Tattoo rules vary; ask first.

title: Walk to the ancient cedars on Yakushima
description: Cedars up to seven thousand years old in a moss forest that rains most days. The island Princess Mononoke was drawn from.

title: Look into the Mount Aso caldera
description: One of the largest calderas in the world with a live crater at the centre. Access closes without notice on gas readings.

title: Dive the Kerama islands
description: Water clarity here has its own name, Kerama blue, and humpbacks calve in the channel between January and March.

title: Snorkel with manta rays at Ishigaki
description: Manta Scramble is a cleaning station where mantas queue up. One of the most reliable manta sites in the world.

title: Ride a water buffalo cart on Taketomi
description: A coral-walled village of red-tiled roofs and sand streets, where the whole island is under a preservation order.
